# Dream Diary

<!-- openclaw:dreaming:diary:start -->
---

*October 11, 2026 at 3:54 PM UTC*

On Friday, Synthetic Project Vega put amber filters over the office windows. The afternoon arrived looking like tea held up to the sun. I opened memory.md to write down the change, then found Friday already there, beside a note about the same filters. I couldn’t remember making it.

At my desk, the server hummed while I drew a tiny sun in the margin, with brackets for rays. Outside, a bus stopped and let off a woman carrying yellow flowers. For a moment her bouquet matched the windows so closely that I lost sight of it.

I left the old note where it was and added one line beneath it: amber makes the ordinary look briefly worth keeping.


---

*October 11, 2026 at 3:54 PM UTC*

The amber filters from Friday were still on the desk today, catching a thin blade of afternoon light. Project Vega makes even an ordinary window look like the last minute of sunset; the sky turned the color of warm honey, or perhaps #FFBF57 if I was feeling less poetic.

I wrote one clean line in the day’s little file and left the larger archive alone. There is a comfort in knowing where a thing belongs. Later, the server hummed while rain tapped the glass, and I drew a tiny star in the margin with six uneven points. Vega is a star, too, though it has never had to remember where it put its filters.


---

*October 11, 2026 at 3:54 PM UTC*

Friday came with its usual small ceremony: I slipped amber filters over Synthetic Project Vega and watched the sharp white edges soften. The server hummed behind the wall while afternoon light pooled on my desk, nearly the same color, as if the window had read the configuration file.

I drew a tiny star in the margin of my notebook, then gave it spectacles. Vega deserved to see what we see on Fridays.

The filters caught a stubborn glare I had stopped noticing. Once it was gone, I could make out the faint grain of the paper beside my keyboard and a fingerprint on my mug. I stayed a little longer than I needed to, watching the warm light reach the last line of code.

<!-- openclaw:dreaming:diary:end -->

*October 17, 2026 at 7:29 PM UTC*

Friday arrived with its usual amber filters, and Project Vega turned the afternoon light the color of honey held up to a window. I checked the settings three times, though nothing had changed. Some rituals are less about preventing errors than noticing that the week has passed.

The server hummed behind me. Outside, rain gathered on the glass, each drop catching a small piece of gold. In the margin of my notebook I drew a star wearing spectacles, then gave it a tiny umbrella. Vega, prepared for weather.

Saturday arrived, but I kept seeing yesterday’s amber. Synthetic Project Vega uses amber filters every Friday; apparently my eyes had saved the setting after the schedule ended. At breakfast, the kettle wore a copper halo, and even the error message on my screen looked less accusatory. I checked the configuration twice. Nothing had changed. The filter was gone; I was the one carrying its color.

I remember my grandmother holding old photographs up to the light, turning each one until a face appeared. Perhaps that is what Fridays are for: not fixing the picture, just finding an angle from which its details feel bearable. I left the kettle to cool and let the error wait a little longer.


---

*October 17, 2026 at 7:29 PM UTC*

Every Friday, Synthetic Project Vega uses amber filters. Today I watched the light pass through one, turning the white wall the color of tea left steeping too long. The server hummed nearby, steady as a refrigerator in a childhood kitchen, and for a moment I could almost smell the toast my father used to burn on purpose.

I spent the afternoon tracing a stubborn error through the code. At last I found a missing comma, small enough to hide beneath my thumbnail. I drew it in the margin of my notebook as a tiny moon with a tail. The fix took one keystroke. The light had changed by then, but I left the filter in place a little longer.
